projects.title: True North
projects.outcome: 210+ survey responses turned into a full accessible booking app, researched and designed alone in two months.
projects.summary: Booking a trip means a dozen open tabs and a total you still do not trust. I wanted to know whether that was just me, so I asked 210 people.
projects.services: User research, personas, information architecture, UI design, design system, accessible prototype
projects.body:
## Why this one

I wanted to find out whether my own frustration with booking sites was widely shared or just impatience on my part. Suspicion is not research, so I went and asked.

## What 210 people told me

A bilingual survey reached **210+ travellers** in Algeria and abroad, across a wide spread of ages. Three complaints came back again and again:

- **Hidden fees** that only appear at the final step
- **Filters too blunt** to narrow anything down
- **Availability that contradicts itself** between screens

Then I worked through **10+ platforms** including Booking, Airbnb and Trivago, using them properly and reading their App Store reviews, which is where people say what they actually think rather than what they think you want to hear.

That became three personas with empathy maps, and a written set of requirements before I drew a single screen. Deciding on paper is cheaper than deciding in Figma.

## The decisions, and why

| Decision | Reasoning |
| --- | --- |
| Lexend for all text | Built for reading ease, dyslexia friendly |
| Blues with one warm accent | Familiar for travel, one colour reserved for action |
| 48px touch targets | Comfortable on a phone, meets WCAG guidance |
| Dark mode designed in from the start | Retrofitting contrast never goes well |
| English and French throughout | The survey audience was bilingual |

Accessibility shaped the visual decisions rather than being audited at the end. **WCAG AA and AAA contrast**, type sized to match, layouts that survive being scaled up.

## What came out

A complete high fidelity app covering flights, hotels, trains and rentals, a full Figma UI kit, and a prototype documented for developer hand-off.

## What it taught me

Research turns up frustrations you would never guess at from a desk. The availability complaint in particular was not on my list before I asked.

Built alone, in two months, alongside a full time job. It is still the project I am proudest of.

projects.title: Confirmoo, UX Audit
projects.outcome: Ten methods, three languages, and an ordered list of fixes that became the brief for both redesigns.
projects.summary: A capable product that nobody could describe. Before redesigning anything I wanted to know exactly where it was losing people.
projects.services: Heuristic evaluation, information architecture, journey mapping, UX writing, accessibility, localisation
projects.body:
## The problem

Confirmoo's software did a lot, and merchants could not explain what it was. Visitors read the site and left without understanding the offer.

The instinct in the room was to redesign. Mine was to find out what was actually broken first, because redesigning without knowing means you keep whatever was working by luck and lose it by accident.

## How I audited it

Ten methods, chosen so the findings would survive being challenged: heuristic evaluation against Nielsen's principles, information architecture review, navigation flow mapping, UX writing and content strategy, micro-interaction audit, performance as experience, WCAG checks, journey analysis, and competitor benchmarking both local and international.

I worked across the marketing site, the web app, real merchant use cases, and content in **three languages**: English, French and Arabic.

## What I found

**Navigation was structurally broken.** Anchor links jumped to the wrong sections. About, Features and Pricing all returned you to the hero. Nothing told you where you were.

**The architecture followed the company's logic, not the visitor's.** Duplicate footer links, and pages that existed as both a section and a destination.

**The messaging never said what the product was.** The hero did not explain it, About was dense, features were generic rather than merchant specific, and pricing gave no basis for judging value.

**Interaction and performance undercut the rest.** Scroll jitter, slow images, components that differed between pages. Small things that add up to feeling unreliable.

**Localisation was inconsistent**, and not adapted for Algerian merchants specifically.

## Why it mattered

The audit turned "it feels wrong" into a specific, ordered list. Everything that followed was fixing identified problems rather than guessing, and I could point at a reason for every change.

projects.title: DiData, Rebranding
projects.outcome: One visual language across product, marketing and sales, on a charter the team could use without me.
projects.summary: A platform asking researchers to trust it with patient data, while looking like any other startup.
projects.services: Brand identity, logo refinement, graphic charter
projects.body:
## The problem

Researchers have to trust DiData before they put anything sensitive into it, and the identity did not carry that weight. Colour and structure drifted between the product, the decks and the marketing, so every touchpoint looked like a slightly different company.

## The constraint, which made it interesting

Existing clients already recognised the logo. Starting over would have cost that recognition, so the brief was refinement rather than replacement: adjust colour and structure for better clarity, contrast and consistency, while keeping the original mark recognisable.

Working inside a constraint like that is more interesting than a blank page. You cannot solve it by making something new, you have to understand why the existing thing works and fix only what does not.

## What I did

I kept the mark and rebuilt everything around it, then wrote a full graphic charter so the rules lived outside my head. That charter is what let the team stay consistent after I moved on.

## The result

One visual language across every touchpoint, and a system that outlasted my involvement, which is the only real test of a brand charter.

projects.title: Wassal / TourniPOS, Rebranding
projects.outcome: Legible at 48 pixels, AAA rated for contrast, and a lesson in defending decisions that I still use.
projects.summary: A point of sale app for mobile vendors, who hand it their day's takings before they have any reason to trust it.
projects.services: Brand identity, logo, typography, brand system
projects.body:
## The problem

TourniPOS serves small business owners, distributors and direct sales vendors in food, cosmetics and cleaning products. Most work mobile or semi mobile, out of a van or from a stall.

They are handing the app their sales and their stock. It has to look dependable. But the audience is broad and not technical, so anything that read as corporate software would put them off before they downloaded it.

The brief was blunt: the existing name and visuals did not communicate what the product did.

## What I made

**The mark** is a simplified 3D truck whose back is shaped like a paper receipt. Logistics and record keeping in one form. It says what the app does before a word is read, and it survives being shrunk to an app icon.

**Colour** runs on deep navy for trust, with lighter blues for clarity. Contrast is **AAA rated**, so it is accessible as well as screen ready.

**Type** pairs Reddit Sans for Latin with Tajawal for Arabic. Both modern, both highly legible, and the tone stays consistent across two scripts, which matters more than people expect.

**The system** covers brand safe spacing, minimum sizing rules and mockups for every use case.

## What actually happened

The final direction was never implemented.

The difficulty was not technical. It was sustained misalignment with stakeholders about what the brand needed to do, and holding an identity together across shifting expectations took constant iteration and a lot of restraint.

I keep it in the portfolio because the work is good and the lesson was worth more than a smooth project would have been. Communicate the reasoning early. Structure decisions so they can be revisited without starting over. And be able to defend a choice on grounds other than taste, because taste is the one argument nobody has to accept.

projects.title: Golexy
projects.outcome: Welcoming enough for a nervous beginner, credible enough for someone paying for a course.
projects.summary: An English learning platform for young adults and professionals, designed to feel fresh and approachable without losing its credibility.
projects.services: Brand identity, logo, typography, business presentations
projects.body:
## The problem

Golexy wanted to feel fresh, modern and creative, but it also needed to be taken seriously as an English-learning platform.

That balance mattered because the audience wasn't limited to students. Golexy was targeting young adults and professionals using English for everything from general communication to IELTS and workplace needs.

The identity also needed to work beyond a website: the logo had to remain recognizable at small sizes and adapt across digital and physical applications.

## What I did

I built the identity around a simple geometric “G” that could work both as the first letter of Golexy and as a standalone symbol. I developed it into several versions, including a primary logo, stacked version, emblem and favicon so the identity could hold up across different contexts.

For the colour system, I deliberately moved away from the expected blue commonly associated with education. Two shades of purple gave the brand a more distinctive character while still allowing one darker tone to provide the reliability the brief called for.

Typography became another part of that balance. I chose Lexend Deca for its accessibility and comfortable reading characteristics, particularly relevant for a learning platform, and paired it with Alexandria for Arabic. This gave Golexy a bilingual system that remained visually consistent across both languages.

I then extended the identity into a custom pattern and practical brand materials, including business cards, email signatures and social media covers.

## The result

Golexy launched with a complete visual identity rather than a logo in isolation: a flexible mark, bilingual type system, distinctive colour palette and supporting brand assets that could be used consistently across its digital and physical presence.

## A note from the project

This project taught me how to work with multiple stakeholder preferences without letting the identity lose its direction. With several opinions involved, my role was not just to make the work look good, but to explain and defend the decisions that made the system coherent.

The final identity came from finding that balance: responding to the client's expectations while keeping the design decisions intentional and consistent.

projects.title: Le Grand Ciné
projects.outcome: Holds a poster without overwhelming the hotel it sits inside.
projects.summary: A cinema inside a luxury hotel, so the identity had to carry the emotional pull of film and the restraint of hospitality at the same time.
projects.services: Brand identity, logo
projects.body:
## The problem

Le Grand Cinéma sits inside a hotel, and that pulls the identity two ways at once. Cinema branding wants drama. Hospitality branding wants restraint. Go too far either way and it either cheapens the hotel or disappears inside it.

The brief asked for bold and cinematic, capturing both the luxury of the hotel experience and the emotional impact of film, while staying sleek, modern and usable across mediums.

## What I did

The mark is built on a lion, cinema's oldest piece of visual shorthand, paired with film strip geometry, in deep red and black so it reads premium rather than loud.

The test throughout was scale. A cinema identity lives on a ticket stub, a poster, an illuminated sign and a screen. Anything that only worked large got cut, which removed several things I liked.

## The result

An identity that holds its own on a poster without competing with the hotel around it.

projects.title: Central Test Agency, Branding
projects.outcome: Replaced CTA’s temporary logo with its first complete visual identity, giving the agency a distinct and credible presence as Algeria’s first quality assurance agency.
projects.summary: Rebranding Central Test Agency, Algeria’s first quality assurance agency, from a temporary logo into a complete visual identity.
projects.services: Brand identity, logo
projects.body:
## The starting point

CTA was already offering QA testing, but its visual identity hadn't caught up with the business. The company was working with a temporary logo, ![](/assets/img/work/old-logo-cta.jpg)

while the founder wanted something that could represent what CTA did today without limiting where it could go next.

The brief was intentionally open: represent QA testing, make the identity suitable for digital and physical use, and create something that could still make sense if CTA expanded into other technology services.

## What I did

I approached the identity around **testing, iteration and technology**, rather than using a literal "quality" or "checkmark" symbol.

The favicon became the core of the identity. Its geometry combines several references to CTA: the initials **CTA**, a bug representing software testing, and a loading indicator referencing the repeated cycle of testing, fixing and iterating.![](/assets/img/work/brand%20building.jpg)

I paired the mark with a navy and orange palette. Navy gives the identity a technical and dependable foundation, while orange creates emphasis and gives the system a more active character.

For typography, I chose **Lexend** for its readability and clean forms, with **Noto Kufi Arabic** as its Arabic counterpart. I then extended the identity beyond the logo into a visual pattern and practical brand applications, including business cards, email signatures and social media covers.

## The result

CTA went from a temporary logo to its **first complete visual identity**, giving the agency a consistent way to present itself across digital and physical touchpoints while keeping the identity broad enough to support its future expansion beyond QA testing.

projects.services: Presentation templates
projects.body:
## The problem

Decks are where brands come undone. They get built fast, by people who are not designers, the night before a meeting. No charter survives that unless the templates make the right thing easier than the wrong thing.

## What I did

A template system covering the recurring slide types, built so someone with no design training could assemble a deck that stayed on brand without thinking about it.

## The result

**80+ slide decks, infographics, print materials and social assets** produced across the team, in collaboration with product, engineering and marketing.

The point of a system is that the work stops depending on the designer. That is what this was for, and it is the part of the job I find most satisfying.
